title: The First Night and the Three Boxes: a Founding Member from Heidelberg to Bronxville
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Heidelberg: born to a chemist in the last German years
stops.date_confidence: Attested. The birth date of 25 February 1931 is given by LA Dance Chronicle and by Wikipedia. The parents' names carried in the research pool as coming from the Black Mountain College Museum page are not on that page, which was refetched and holds only a one-line description, the summer sessions, the company dates and Sarah Lawrence: Eduard Farber's name and Jewish identity rest on LA Dance Chronicle alone, and the mother's name given in the pool as Dora Schmidt Farber is unsourced and is dropped here.
stops.campa: Viola Farber is born in Heidelberg on the twenty-fifth of February, daughter of the chemist Eduard Farber. The household is a musical one and she will be a serious pianist long before she is anything else; a family that performs together as a quartet is the ordinary furniture of her childhood. Germany in 1931 is two years from the Nuremberg laws and her father is a Jew. She has seven years in the city of her birth, and no school, teacher or first recital is recorded for any of them. What the record holds is the piano in the house.
sources: Jeff Slayton, 'Dance History Needs to Remember Viola Farber (1931-1998),' LA Dance Chronicle
Wikipedia, 'Viola Farber'
Dorothea Rockburne, oral history interview, Black Mountain College Museum + Arts Center
suggested_refs: The Farber family quartet, known only from Rockburne's recollection of what Farber told her at Black Mountain

stops.name: New Haven: the family comes ashore
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by LA Dance Chronicle, which gives the flight from Nazi restrictions and the New Haven then Washington path. Month and day are placeholders. The account that Eduard Farber's employer arranged the exit is Slayton's and has no second source.
stops.campa: The Farbers get out of Germany in 1938 and come ashore in Connecticut. Slayton's account holds that Eduard Farber's employer arranged the exit before emigration closed further; the family does not stay long in New Haven. Viola is seven years old and arrives without English into a country that will keep her for sixty years. Of the crossing itself, the ship, the port, the papers, the money, nothing survives in any source reachable here. The next address on record is Washington.
sources: Jeff Slayton, 'Dance History Needs to Remember Viola Farber (1931-1998),' LA Dance Chronicle
suggested_refs: Emigration records for Eduard Farber, chemist, 1938, not located in any reachable database

stops.name: Washington: the refugee child and Erika Thimey
stops.date_confidence: The range given by LA Dance Chronicle is 1938 to about 1949. The single 1940 date is a placeholder to order the segment and is not attested for any particular event. Thimey's studio address was not located.
stops.campa: The family settles in the capital and the refugee child grows up American there. She studies modern dance with Erika Thimey, herself a German emigre teaching in Washington, and she keeps at the piano with the seriousness of somebody who expects to make a living from it. Dance is the second study, not the first. The eleven years between arrival and university are otherwise blank: no school named, no recital, no photograph, no account of what it was to be a German Jewish child in Washington through the war. Where Thimey's studio stood is not recorded either.
sources: Jeff Slayton, 'Dance History Needs to Remember Viola Farber (1931-1998),' LA Dance Chronicle
suggested_refs: Erika Thimey's Washington dance studio and her German expressionist training, the first modern dance Farber saw

stops.name: Urbana: a music major takes her first dance class
stops.date_confidence: About 1948 to 1949, per Wikipedia and LA Dance Chronicle, which agree on Illinois as a music major under Margaret Erlanger and on a transfer back to Washington after a year. September is a placeholder for the academic year.
stops.campa: She enrolls at the University of Illinois as a music major and takes her first formal dance classes there, under Margaret Erlanger. One year is all it lasts. The piano is still the career and the dancing is still the elective, but the elective is what keeps her in the studio after hours. Whether she finished any coursework, or what she played at her juries, or what Erlanger made of her, is not in the record. She leaves Urbana without a degree and goes back to Washington to keep studying both at once.
stops.quote: She was a very all-around person. She didn't start out as a dancer.
stops.quote_source: Dorothea Rockburne, oral history interview, Black Mountain College Museum + Arts Center

stops.campa: Back in Washington she continues as a music major and adds dance study to it. Which campus took her is not settled: one account names American University, another names George Washington, and the two are left standing against each other. No degree from either school appears anywhere, and neither registrar was consulted this pass. She is nineteen, still officially a musician, still living in the city her parents fled to, and still taking the dancing as the lesser of her two studies.

stops.name: Black Mountain College: the stone house and the broken butterfly
stops.date_confidence: The Black Mountain College Museum + Arts Center gives two discrete summer sessions, 1951 and 1953, not continuous enrollment; the word transfer, used throughout the pool, is wrong and is not used here. Wikipedia's 'by 1952' is not a third source for residence. The much repeated story that she came after seeing a photograph of Cunningham dancing with Anneliese Widman is not in the Rockburne interview cited for it, which was read in full, and could not be sourced anywhere; it is left out. Pin inherited byte for byte from merce_cunningham.journey.json and john_cage.journey.json.
stops.campa: She comes to Black Mountain for the summer session and lodges in one of the stone houses, sharing a room with the painter Dorothea Rockburne. She studies with Katherine Litz, whose way of moving Rockburne remembers as a broken butterfly, and she goes into Merce Cunningham's classes alongside her roommate. The college is broke and the faculty is famous. What arrives here is not a dance student but an accomplished musician who has been dancing on the side for three years. She will come back for one more summer, in 1953, and that is the whole of her time at the college.
stops.quote: We both went into Merce's classes together, and she was an accomplished pianist and her family was used to performing as a quartet.
stops.quote_source: Dorothea Rockburne, oral history interview, Black Mountain College Museum + Arts Center

stops.date_confidence: Attested by the Merce Cunningham Trust production record for Banjo, which gives 21 August 1953 and the full original cast. stops.campa: On the twenty-first of August, in the second of her two summers at the college, the Merce Cunningham Dance Company gives its first program, and Farber is in it. She dances Banjo with Carolyn Brown, Remy Charlip, Cunningham, Jo Anne Melsher and Paul Taylor, to Gottschalk played live by David Tudor. She is not a later recruit to a repertory; she is on the first night, a founding member of a company that will run for fifty-six years. She is twenty-two, and she stays thirteen of them.

stops.campa: Outside the company she dances the vampire in Katherine Litz's Dracula, opposite Charles Weidman, keeping a second and older experimental line open beside Cunningham's. She is taking ballet in these years from Margaret Craske and Alfred Corvino, and she has danced with Paul Taylor's early company as well. The Cunningham dancer of the fifties is not a specialist bred inside one school. She is a musician who trained late and takes class wherever the class is good. stops.name: New York: Crises, and the elastic bands
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Farber originated roles in Crises, Rune and Nocturnes, per LA Dance Chronicle. The Caines phrase is verbatim but reaches this file through Wikipedia, which quotes the International Encyclopedia of Dance entry; the encyclopedia page itself could not be opened, and the pool's oxford-dance.com citation path is fabricated and is not used.
stops.campa: She originates roles in Crises, in Rune, in Nocturnes. She is the dancer Cunningham hands the off-balance material to, the awkward phrasing, the passages that look about to fall over; the encyclopedias settle on the word individualist for what she does with them. Seven years into the company, she has still made no dance of her own. In Crises the dancers are joined to one another by elastic bands, and holding a line taut against another body is the kind of problem she is good at.
stops.quote: one of the great individualists of the company

Her students learn the vocabulary from somebody who was in the room while it was being made. Technique class is also the pay: a company dancer's week is built around the classes that fund the performing. The years for this come from one tertiary chronology, roughly 1961 to 1969, and no studio record was reachable to hold it to a date or an address.

stops.campa: John Cage assembles a relay of pianists to play Erik Satie's Vexations through all eight hundred and forty repetitions, and Farber takes her turn at the keyboard. She has been a Cunningham dancer for ten years, and here she is hired for the piano. The published roster names twelve players, Cage, David Tudor, Christian Wolff, Philip Corner, John Cale, Joshua Rifkin and the rest, and she is the only woman among them. The performance runs about eighteen hours, from the evening of the ninth into the following afternoon.

Farber is on it, dancing a repertory she has helped make for eleven years, in cities with no idea what they are about to be shown. Paris receives it as a scandal and an event at once, which is the reception the company gets used to. It is her first working visit to a city she will keep coming back to for thirty years. She is thirty-three, and she has about eighteen months left in the company.

stops.name: New York: leaving the company
stops.date_confidence: 1965 given by both LA Dance Chronicle and Wikipedia. Month and day are placeholders. No source consulted documents a cause; both describe a transition to independent choreography.
stops.campa: After thirteen years she leaves the Merce Cunningham Dance Company. No source consulted records a quarrel, a firing or a scandal; both of the accounts that exist describe a dancer moving on to her own work. She is thirty-four, has been in the company since before it had a name, and has never made a dance. Cunningham keeps her teaching in his studio afterwards. What she does with the next five years is thinly documented, and even the year her own company begins is disputed.

stops.name: Garden City: the Adelphi faculty, and the day job

stops.campa: She joins the dance faculty at Adelphi on Long Island, an hour out from the city, and teaches modern technique to undergraduates. This is the part of a dancer's life nobody photographs: the train out, the studio with the bad floor, the students who will not become dancers. It pays, and she will keep some version of it for the rest of her working life. When the appointment began is disputed. Slayton gives 1966; a reference chronology opens the range in 1959, six years before she left Cunningham, and neither is preferred here.

stops.campa: She teaches a year at Bennington, at the college that had been American modern dance's summer laboratory a generation before her. She is between things: out of the company, not yet running one, carrying a vocabulary into rooms where it is still news. One line in a reference chronology gives the years. No institutional document was reachable to confirm them, and no student, class or work made in that year is named anywhere. Whether she was hired to teach Cunningham's technique or something already her own, no source consulted says.

stops.name: New York: the company takes her name
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction left standing: Wikipedia dates the company's beginning to 1968, LA Dance Chronicle to 1970. Both are reported and neither is preferred; 1970 orders the segment. The quote is Slayton's, from LA Dance Chronicle.
stops.campa: She forms a company around herself and it takes her name. What she asks of it is the reverse of the usual demand: not that the dancers reproduce her, but that the piece come out different because these particular people are in it. Slayton, who dances in it and marries her, says her work had more to do with the people dancing it than Cunningham's did. The music is not fastened to the steps either; if a dance has internal or set musical cues, they change the music.
stops.quote: She taught us to dance like individuals, not like carbon copies of her
stops.quote_source: Jeff Slayton, 'Dance History Needs to Remember Viola Farber (1931-1998),' LA Dance Chronicle

stops.name: New York: the marriage and the partnership are one object
stops.date_confidence: 1971 attested by Slayton in LA Dance Chronicle, who writes only that they were married from 1971 to 1980. Month and day are placeholders. The pool's detail that the wedding was in the Garden Room at Judson Church is unsourced: the word Judson does not appear in the article cited for it, so the venue is dropped and the generic New York pin used.
stops.campa: She marries Jeff Slayton, who dances in her company and partners her in most of it. Where the wedding took place is not recorded in anything reachable, and the one detail in circulation about it does not survive checking. The marriage and the working partnership are the same object; there is no version of the next decade in which one of them runs without the other. They will separate before the marriage formally ends, and go on dancing together for eighteen years after that, to a last shared performance in 1996.

stops.name: Fort Worth: a dance made for the camera
stops.date_confidence: The Rauschenberg Foundation's performance history labels the television production 1976 and the gallery preview and broadcast 1977; both years sit on the same page and both are reported here rather than reconciled. Coordinates approximate the Fort Worth Art Museum; the KERA studios are in Dallas and no single pin covers the production.
stops.campa: The Fort Worth Art Museum and KERA Channel 13 put up a television dance, and Farber makes Brazos River for the camera. Robert Rauschenberg, whom she has known since the Black Mountain summers, does the sets and costumes; David Tudor, who played Gottschalk at her first performance in 1953, writes an electronic score; Dan Parr directs. The company dances it: Jumay Chu, Larry Clark, Willi Feuer, June Finch, Anne Koren, Susan Matheke, Ande Peck, Slayton and Farber herself.

stops.name: Leo Castelli Gallery: a dance premiered on a SoHo wall
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the Robert Rauschenberg Foundation performance history for 28 March 1977 at 420 West Broadway.
stops.campa: Brazos River is shown at Leo Castelli's gallery on West Broadway on the twenty-eighth of March, in a room built for paintings, to an art audience rather than a dance audience. This is Rauschenberg's constituency more than hers, and it is the constituency that will remember the piece. Farber has spent her whole career adjacent to the visual arts, from Black Mountain forward, without ever being quite claimed by them. A dance made for a Texas public television station gets its New York premiere hanging on a SoHo wall, at 420 West Broadway, on a Monday in March.

Within twelve months she will be living in France, and the New York company that carried her own name for a decade will be finished.
